analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "This is submitted. We'll hear arguments next in Russell against the United States. Yes. Mr. Ackles, I think you may proceed whenever you're ready. Mr. Chief Justice, may we please record. The issue in this case is a simple issue, but the resolution is a little more complex. The issue is whether or not under section 844 subparagraph I of title 18 United States code, a building which was a two-flat residential building, which the defendant petitioner here attempted to commit arson, is covered by the language of the statute. That states that anyone who attempts to destroy a building, I'm sorry, anybody who attempts to strike any building used in interstate or foreign commerce or in an activity affecting interstate or foreign commerce commits the crime. To determine legislative intent, this court frequently does look at the congressional hearings to determine what the proponents of the bill or the law stated. Briefly, the facts are that in February of 1983, the petitioner here owned a two-flat residential building, one of which was occupied. The flat was rented by a family paying $235 a month. It was a two-flat building, not used for any commercial activity or business enterprise. The language of the representatives in passing the legislation stated that they're passing this legislation to prevent generally organized crime because it was legislation during the organized crime legislation of the general nature. And they prohibited the destruction of any property used for business purposes. That's not in the statute, but that's in the congressional discussion by the representatives. And so the question here is whether this two-flat building, which is not used for a business purpose, was covered under the statute. The government has pointed out in its brief that there were further hearings in which the language was deleted when they said only business purposes. And then they said only any building because they wanted to include churches, schools, and police stations within the protection from being bombed or from being bombed. Well, when the Congress then, when the legislators stated that we will just say any building and that should cover churches, schools, and police stations, it did not cover, it did not state, they did not state that. It also covers residential buildings. Counsel, you stated that the building was not used for any commercial or business purpose. Is it a fact that business insurance was carried on the building? Well, the petitioner had insurance covering a fire loss. It wasn't identified as, it wasn't stated in the policy business fire loss, it was just fire loss to a building. But the same type of insurance you would have on your own residence? Yes. What about the deduction of expenses for tax purposes? This defendant owned three other two flat buildings, separate and distinct, not conjoined, at separate places in Chicago, Illinois. He received rent from them, he put the income on his income tax, he deducted depreciation, he deducted interest, he did that. On this building? On this building also. Right. On this building, the building is not a property for business purposes. It is our contention. The government suggests to your honor that later in 1982, the act was amended to include the word fire. That is, the initial act passed in 1970, merely precluded a building from being destroyed by means of explosive. Three courts of appeals held that the commission of an ordinary fire on a building was not included within the concept of the term explosive. So they had further hearings. So they had further hearings to get around or to overrule the three separate circuit courts that had ruled that committing a fire, putting gasoline, putting a torch to the gasoline and burning a building was not included in the concept of explosive. So they wanted to make more certain that the law would encompass a fire. So in 1980, they held hearings. And as the solicitor general, so helpful to the petitioner, sets out in his brief on page 18 footnote 20, it calls to the attention of this court that the Congress included the only amendment to the section 844 subparagraph I is the inclusion of the word fire, which is not in the previous statute. And they held hearings about the inclusion. And its purpose, as the government points out to your honors, is to overcome the three circuit court holdings that fire was not an explosive. So they put in the word fire. So there's a question that fire is included in the concept of the criminal statute. Well, they knew, that is, the Congress knew at that time that the case of United States versus Minuti, which we largely or in large part rely, was decided in 1981 by the Second Circuit Judge Friendly writing the opinion. And Judge Friendly, writing for the Second Circuit, held under circumstances analogous to this one, that the burning of a building or the explosion of a building, not a building, owned by Minuti, which was used for residential purposes, where he received rent from it, where he presumably reported that on income tax, deducted depreciation. If he paid interest, that that would be a deduction, was not included in the concept of building because, said Mr. Justice Friendly, Judge Friendly, that the Congress intended in 1970 to include only buildings used for business purposes. But his opinion was based on the plain language of the statute, wasn't it? I'm sorry, sir? Wasn't his opinion based on the plain language of the statute? No, your honor, Mr. Justice Marshall. It was based because the legislators had stated in their discussions about passing the law that the buildings were considered to be only for business purposes. The government points out that really there was more discussion and the legislators in 1970 discussed including churches used in commerce, in quotes, from the statute. Well, Mr. Justice Friendly stated that the fact that the government intended to use as a nexus for federal jurisdiction, the fact that the building in Minuti used electricity or gas was an insufficient, improper and impermissible nexus upon which to apply federal jurisdiction. He said that the word building means only business property. It does not mean rental or residential property. That's how he interpreted the word building because of the legislative hearings stating that the building here considered in 1970 was to be only business purposes. And that is why, Mr. Justice Marshall and justices, when the Congress amended the statute to include the word fire where it was not in the statute before, and when they specifically passed that law to overcome three separate circuit court opinions that fire was not included within the concept of explosive, knowing what the law was then, I assume the staff of the Congress advised them advised them what the law is, they knew that the law was then, they knew that the law was then, they knew that the second circuit at least, had decided that When did this revision that you're talking about take place, Mr. Eccles? 1982. I don't know the specific month. But the year after Minuti was decided. Yes, sir. Minuti was decided in 1981. Again, I don't have the specific month. I would assume that the researchers advising the legislators with respect to the three circuits about fire, fire not being included explosive, would have advised the Congress about the Minuti decision. So they had that knowledge. And, says the government in its helpful footnote 20, the House report provided that, I quote, jurisdictional circumstances enumerated in that section, 844i, shall otherwise remain unchanged. That is, it is my respectful presentation to your honors that, with the legislators knowing, they had to know of the Minuti decision, they didn't change any circumstance of 844i except to add the word fire. Well, the government argues that even if residential property is excluded, they don't say that it is excluded, but even if it is excluded, that this is not residential property, it's business property, because of the fact that he received income, reported it on as income tax, made deductions for depreciation and deductions for interest, that therefore this is a business property. But that doesn't end the question. There has to be a federal nexus. There has to be federal interstate activity, because the statute... So, would you say that a 40-unit apartment building would give jurisdiction under this statute? Yes. As a matter of fact, there was a case discussed in both of our briefs, the Zabek case, out of my home circuit, the 7th circuit. Well, what number of leased apartments do you think essential before there is jurisdiction that there be? Don't know, can't answer, but at least a key flat building is a residential building, and even though he gets income from it, it's a residential building and not a commercial property of 44 apartments. One of the 7th circuit said that there are other characteristics of interstate character, the supplies contributed to the building had to come from out of state, and there's a 13 or 14 apartment building in the very recently decided cases coming out of Nebraska. Well, I guess it's hard for me to see why not a two-unit building. Well, your honor has to decide it eventually, and if you cannot see it, then I cannot give you the vision with which to see. But a two-flat residential building is not generally considered, I don't consider it, commercial business property. Both of the flats were rented? No, well, the first, he did not live in that one. He lived someplace else with his family in a home in another part of the city. The second floor flat was rented at $235 a month. The first floor flat was unrented at the time. Whether both were rented at the time or both were entered at the time, I don't think changes the legal posture. Well, you have the argument to make in response to the government's claim that the use of natural gas from interstate commerce fulfills the... that no natural gas heating was perhaps being used while they were unoccupied. Well, I thank your honor for that question because that gives me an added argument for your honors. I'm glad for the help. Does it make any difference then whether the two-flat is vacant temporarily or whether both flats are occupied? Does that take it out of or into the federal concept? It's not difficult to make a conundrum out of this case. I don't know how far that gets us along to the road to deciding it. In any event, every circuit that has had this question, that is, the question whether or not the use of gas or the use of electricity takes it into the federal jurisdiction, has ruled against it. In a very recent case decided just two months ago, United States versus Hansen and Terlecki, two separate defendants, I think the apartments there were 14 apartments. The apartments were in North Dakota on the border of Nebraska. But that building said the court, the 8th circuit had transients. The building was used clearly for interstate purposes. It had interstate transients going to and from the building from Nebraska. They were day tenants. And the 8th circuit said, we will not go as far as the 7th circuits in using the concept that the 14 apartment buildings had electricity that was generated from out of North Dakota as a basis for federal jurisdiction. They said specifically, we will not go as far as Russell. Russell, by that time, had been decided. Russell was decided last July of 1984. Hansen and Terlecki was decided in February, about 10 days or two weeks before I submitted the brief to this court. They said, we are not going to buy that concept that the use of electricity takes it into the federal concept. And other cases have similarly held. The Manuti case held in the face of the government argument that even though it is a residential property and even though there is income derived from it, benefit derived from it, it is not business property. And we won't permit, said Manuti, that the use of electricity to that building had to get electricity generated by power, generated by gas coming in from out of state. As in this case, they proved that the gas used on the second floor started in Oklahoma or Texas, met its terminus in Joliet, Illinois, mixed with other gas and finally got into the building through the pipeline. Manuti said, we're not going to use that concept. That's not a proper federal nexus. Barton case from the Second Circuit, which held the defendant guilty of torching a gambling establishment, said that that gambling establishment, it discussed Manuti. It said, we don't hold that because the gambling establishment, which is a business-related building, a business-purpose-related building, we don't hold that because that got electricity, that that takes it in. In that aspect, Barton in the Second Circuit agreed with Manuti in the Second Circuit. It said that supplies were delivered to the gambling establishment for the benefit of the gambling customers, such as orange juice or drinks, and that had as its genesis an out-of-New York beginning. So that the courts have rejected it. There's another interesting case. Interesting to judges, of course, because there, in United States versus Manholland, Eighth Circuit, a truck being driven by a sitting circuit judge, a state judge, was being driven. There was an attempt to bomb the truck. The fellow was convicted because the 844I statute has within it not only the protection of buildings but also vehicles. Well, a pickup truck is driven by a person. Judge or no judge is a vehicle. The bomb was attempted to destroy it. The gas used in the car had its genesis, its origin, out of state. Manholland, Eighth Circuit, said, no, no. We're not going to permit you to expand federal jurisdiction here, even though they acknowledged that the gas used in the truck had as its origin an out-of-state place. So Manholland, Barton, Manuti, and the latest of the cases, Hanson and Terlicki from the Eighth Circuit, decided two months ago in February, rejected the concept that the use of electricity or gas in a building, is sufficient for the federal nexus. Well, what else do I have? In the two cases that I cite, the Lewis case and the Bass case, where we say that where a statute is confusing, it is certainly not clear. If Manholland rejected the government's concept that the statute covers the acts in Manholland, if Manuti rejected the concept of the government, that the use of interstate, that the use of gas coming from interstate brings it into the federal concept, then, and if Hanson and Terlicki, by, I suppose, over to Dicta, because it wasn't an issue then, but it simply stated it wouldn't go so far as the Seventh Circuit in Russell in holding an interstate nexus. If those courts said that, then there's certainly an ambiguity in the statute. And two cases from this court, Ruiz and Bass, Ruiz and Bass, suggest that under those circumstances, the concept of validity should be applicable, and your honor should hold that because the statute isn't clear with respect to applying to the facts in this case, there should be a reversal in this case. Another factor. In its reply brief, in its excellent reply brief, the statement of the statute is not clear with respect to the facts in this case, there should be a reversal in this case. Another factor. In its reply brief, in its excellent reply brief, I say excellent because I respectfully submit that it's helpful to the petitioner in this case, the government points out that in the second set of hearings, in the 1982 hearings, where the Congress was putting in the word fire, where it was not in the status before, that agents of the alcohol, tobacco, and alcohol, tobacco, and firearms unit testified, and they testified that they need the word fire in there because it permits them to go against organized crime units, people in organized crime want to torch places for whatever reasons, for whatever multiple reasons people do that kind of thing. And they said, we want this legislation, and we're not preempting the states. The states still have the power to prosecute. Well, that may be true that the state has the power to prosecute, and in Illinois we have arson statutes, effective, used all the time, and in a case such as this, the punishment if guilt were to be found, would be a minimum mandatory punishment of six to a maximum of 30 years. Even more severe than the fellow has got now. So I don't know if I may be doing any good if I'm able to persuade your honors to reverse, because here he has a 10-year sentence. He is serving that 10-year sentence since he was convicted by the district judge in Chicago. So it is not true that they are only interested in organized crime groups in having the legislation passed. But that is what they said. This is an individual having no organization, having no connection with anybody, who simply decided to torch a building that he owned. I suppose it is a proper inference to say for profit, because he did have insurance on it. Although that was not shown by any evidence in the record. The government said that one of the motives, and one of the motives he had in burning it was to get the proceeds from an insurance policy, and that therefore, because he had the motive, that takes it into the federal nexus because that's fraud against an insurance company. So far as the facts of this case are concerned, so what? There is not a word of evidence that a claim was put in because the building was not burned. There was an attempt burning. That fact is not in dispute at this level. He would have had to use the mails. Well, sometimes in mail fraud cases where insurance companies are the victims, the claimant goes to the insurance company, and that's happened many times in Chicago. I participated in cases where that has occurred, where the claim is physically presented to the insurance company, and the person benefited goes to pick up the check. The mails are not even used. It's fraud, but it's not mail fraud. And so there is a guess, a future guess about future contemplation that the government argues that your honor should consider in accepting the federal nexus that the statute is complied with when the statute states that it must not only be a building, but it must be in an activity affecting interstate or foreign commerce. At trial level, this was a bench trial. Much of the evidence was not in dispute. Most of the evidence was not in dispute. It was a law question. There were insurance policies put into the evidence over my objections, and nonetheless the judge accepted a stipulation that was not stipulated to, but I make no argument before this court. I was the trial lawyer. I was the losing trial lawyer. I was the losing lawyer in the Seventh Circuit, and I hope not in this case. But there was no presentation in those policies that he did anything yet except that there was a contemplation that he would do something. I've asked the marshal to flash me so that I can keep some time for rebuttal. Thank you very much. Thank you. Mr. Wright. Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court, the essential difference between the government and petitioner concerns Congress's intent. Petitioner contends that Congress, in adopting Section 844I, intended to prohibit the destruction of business property only. Furthermore, petitioner defines business property narrowly. The government, in contrast, contends that Congress intended to prohibit the destruction of any building, including business property, as long as a minimal connection is established between the use of the building and commerce. The language, structure, and legislative history all support the government's reading. Section 844I states that it prohibits the destruction of any building used in any activity affecting commerce. If Congress had intended to limit the section's coverage, in the manner petitioner suggests, it could have prohibited the destruction of any business property. But it did not. Mr. Wright, is it the government's contention here that it's the second part of that descriptive language, or in any activity affecting interstate or foreign commerce that covers the property here in question? Excuse me, Justice Rehnquist. Well, as I read the statute, it says, whoever burns real or personal property used in interstate or foreign commerce, or in any activity affecting interstate or foreign commerce. Does the government claim that it comes under the second of those two? Yes, we rely on the affecting commerce plan rather than the commerce plan. And what does the government say is the activity that this building was used in, which affected commerce? Well, we suggest three activities that the building was used in that affect commerce. The gas was used to heat the building. The building was used for rental purposes. And it was insured. Would you say that what activity does the building become used in by reason? The fact that it heats with gas that comes from out of state. Does that put it in a separate activity? The activity is simply the use of heat, and it affects commerce in that if the building is destroyed, the shipment of gas interstate would be reduced. That, of course, is our broadest argument. And it is clear that in this case, had the one two-unit apartment been destroyed, the effect on commerce would have been slight in this case. But arson is not uncommon, as the evidence before Congress in 1982 clearly shows, so that the effect on commerce would be substantial in the aggregate over the class of cases of arsons. There is certainly a lot of traditional law that says a piece of real property that is simply sitting in Chicago or somewhere else is not in interstate commerce. The building is not in commerce, and that is why we are under the second phrase, as you noted, the affecting commerce phrase. We believe it was used not in commerce, but in three activities affecting commerce. Well, why, it was a piece of rental property, wasn't it? Yes, it was. Used for a business purpose. That is one of our three contentions. That's why we believe that petitioner gave us. Well, why isn't that the activity? And then the activity affects commerce because the activity needs to be, the building that is being used in this activity needs to be heated. You do not need to go to our gas ground. You could simply decide this case on the fact that the building was rented and hold that that is enough to bring the building into an activity affecting commerce, and if that is enough, you do not need to go farther, Justice White. How much do you rely on us to write on the fact that it was insured by an insurer in another state and that the whole transaction of making the claim, the false claim, had an impact? Well, that, of course, does make the interstate nexus more clear. However, we would contend that, especially with an insurance company like Allstate, that even if Allstate didn't have multiple offices in many states, that its activity is affected. You think this just buttresses your case, then? Yes. And I might note in that connection, Justice Powell asked whether the building was insured with a homeowner's policy or a business policy. As examination of footnote three in a brief indicates, the Court of Appeals found, as did the district court, that it was a business insurance policy, not a homeowner's policy. Mr. Wright, it would be hard to imagine any building that wouldn't fall under the coverage of this section under the government's test. Certainly under our broadest reading, let me suggest that that fits Congress's intent. When Congress deleted the business purposes phrase from the statute, it did so in response to testimony from a number of congressmen that churches, schools, and private dwellings, I might add, as we note in our brief, Congressman Wiley, and I believe Congressman Goldwater as well mentioned private dwellings, would not necessarily be considered business property, and Congress wanted to cover those. It is, imagine a case that involved a band of terrorists who were burning churches and perhaps the home of church officials and schools run by the church. Evidence gathered by the FBI or the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, and Firearms might only link the terrorists to a particular building. Evidence might only be firm in one case, and if that building did not happen to be rented or did not happen to be used for rental purposes, we maintain it would still be used in an activity affecting commerce if gas or electricity was used in the building. We believe Congress deleted the business purposes phrase in order to cover such a case. We don't expect such a case would arise with great frequency, but it is possible, and that's why we think Congress broadened the phrase, cover other kinds of buildings. Congress knew that by using the affecting commerce language that it was sweeping broadly. This court recognized that in Scarborough, where it said that Congress knows that when it uses that language, it is exerting its power to the full extent of its commerce power. In fact, Congress made quite clear that it was exerting its power to the full extent of the commerce power. It said that in the 1970 House report. It said, we intend to exercise, quote, the fullest jurisdictional breadth constitutionally permissible under the commerce clause. The representative who introduced the bill containing Section 844i stated that it was broadened, quote, to extend to the full extent of our constitutional power. Petitioners conceded that under the commerce power, Congress may prohibit the destruction of a building like this. Congress rarely states its intention so clearly to go to the full extent of a power, like the commerce power. Section 844i also supports the government's contention here. Examination of that statute, which covers threats to destroy property, makes it illegal to threaten, quote, through the use of the mail, telephone, telegraph, or other instrument of commerce to threaten to destroy any building. It's clear there's no use in an activity affecting commerce language in that section. Is that set forth somewhere in your brief, Mr. 844e? Yes. I'm not sure whether the entire section is set forth in our brief. It's very similar to the language. It prohibits the destruction of any building, vehicle, or other real or personal property, and it uses the nexus to commerce phrase that I just quoted. The United States to be fears is the only case that I know of decided under that statute, which held that it covered threats to destroy a private residence, not even one used for rental purposes as far as the case indicates. The logical conclusion to be drawn from examination of the structure of the statute is that, as in the flyer on the statute that issued in Scarborough, Congress intended that any minimal nexus between a building and commerce should satisfy the jurisdictional requirement. It used the instrument of commerce requirement. Just the red section, subsection E, which I hadn't read before, and I notice it doesn't qualify the word building by the building being used in commerce or in an activity effect just as any building. That is correct. So it's perfectly clear that that would be covered. That's correct. And the... Now, doesn't that sort of cut against you when you contrast that language with the qualifying language that describes the kind of building in subsection I? No, we believe that that language, as a court recognized in Scarborough, is really a jurisdictional statement, a statement that a nexus to commerce is required and a very minimal nexus, and that the instrument of commerce language is used in 844E simply to indicate that, and that an effect in commerce language is used in 844I. To the contrary, it seems to us that it would make no sense to hold that Congress was more interested in threats than it was in actual destruction. And since a threat to burn down this building, if made through the telephone, would have been covered by 844E, we think an actual attempt to destroy it should be covered... Well, of course, the threats they're talking about in E involve a threat of killing, injuring, and intimidating individuals, whereas this one just deals with a property offense. Whereas the threats in E are a little more serious. I mean... Well, anyway, I guess we don't decide on the basis. May I just ask you this question? Which of your three theories that you have do you think would apply to the Manuti case? Would you apply them all to require a different result in Manuti? Certainly application of the gas. That clearly would. Ty would. The rental property is, frankly, much less clear. There was some indication in Manuti that there was an intention to rent that residence at some time in the future. Frankly, a fair reading of the case indicates that Judge Friendly would not have found the requisite tie, I think. But he wasn't really faced with that case there. I think what I may be asking is whether, at the search stage, very, very properly, you suggested there was really no conflict with Manuti. The cases were distinguishable. Are you now asking us, in effect, to disapprove of Manuti? Yes. We are. We presume that, in granting suture area, you decided that the cases are not fairly indistinguishable, which a broad reading of that case indicates. The four justices, so decided. Yes. At least four justices. Mr. Wright, you don't contend that this particular conviction is sustainable under 844E, do you? No, we do not. Petitioner relies heavily on a phrase in the House report that describes Section 844I in arguing that Congress intended to reach business property only. The report, right after the statement that Section 844I represents Congress's full exercise of its commerce power, describes the provision as, quote, a very broad provision covering substantially all business property. The government, of course, does not quarrel with that, the accuracy of that statement. The section is a very broad provision, and substantially all business property is covered by it. But the government does not believe that the phrase was intended to limit Section 844I's coverage. Of course, a phrase in a committee report cannot rewrite a statute. That is especially true where here Congress specifically considered the exact limitation proposed by petitioner and rejected it in order to broaden the statute's coverage and stated that it's so intended by doing it. You're saying that having rental property with four or five tenancies for purposes of this statute is essentially the same as the operation of the Drake Hotel, for example, or the Palmer House in Chicago. We contend that the destruction of both would be covered by the statute. In the case of a large hotel, the effect on interstate commerce from such a destruction would be greater, although I might add that the destruction of any one building has to have a slight effect on commerce, given the magnitude of interstate commerce. But arson is common. Petitioner concedes that a 43-unit apartment building affects commerce. 22-unit apartment buildings, the destruction of 22-unit apartment buildings would logically also affect commerce. Our argument is an aggregation argument, that in the aggregate, destruction of rental property of buildings affects commerce. Of the three ties we've suggested between this building and interstate commerce, the evidence considered by Congress most clearly shows the impact that insurance fraud arson has on interstate commerce. At the 1982 hearings leading to the amendment of Section 844, Congress heard testimony of insurance industry officials who estimated that fires caused $1.3 billion in damage in 1979 alone, and that a substantial portion of all fires are set to defraud insurance companies. Congress noted that the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, and Firearms had saved over $54 million in false claims in 1980 by detecting arson schemes. In this case, Petitioner would have obtained $40,000 in insurance proceeds by destroying his building. That by itself is not trivial. In the aggregate, it is clear that this sort of insurance fraud arson has a major impact on interstate commerce. May I just ask on your insurance theory, is it your position that the statute, just confining myself to that theory, covers every insured building or only every insured building in which the arson is committed by the holder of the insurance, the owner of the insurance policy? We would favor the broader theory. You could confine yourself to a narrower motivation theory, which would cover, of course, not just if any... So your view is every insured building is covered by the statute? That the building is used in an activity affecting commerce, both when it's insured and when it is burned. The other uses... What activity is it being used in when it's insured that distinguishes it from activities that uninsured buildings are used in? Simply the activity of going out and purchasing the insurance policy on the building. So you import an extremely flexible meaning to the word activity, to say the least. Yes, we do. We believe that Congress meant that phrase, used in any activity affecting commerce, to signify that it was going to the full extent of its commerce power. And we believe that Scarborough and other decisions of this case, this court, rather, including the Reliance Fuel Company case, which was cited in the House report right after it stated that Congress intended to exercise its full jurisdictional reach, show that that phrase has the broadest reach. You don't go to the extent of the third theory that Judge Friendly talked about of a class of activities, a member of the class. A specific example might not affect interstate commerce, but if the entire class does, it's also covered under the Pereira cases. You don't say they went that far. They didn't use the full extent to that. Well, Congress could have drafted this statute, I believe you're suggesting, in another way. It could have left off what I call the jurisdictional nexus phrase, and perhaps under Perez would have had to beef up the findings required to show the nexus. But we believe that that phrase was added simply to require the showing of a slate effect on Congress.
